newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr resurgent as offshore funds return.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr resurgent as offshore funds return.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in a blistering rally Tuesday, climbing a cent to two-month highs.

The initial surge came offshore as bids from U.S. investment banks put the squeeze on a short market and reached a crescendo when upbeat domestic data showed the economy was responding to past rate cuts and further stimulation was not needed.

"The landscape has changed and the market is looking at the Aussie in a more favourable light," remarked Steve Shuster, head of forex at Citibank Australia, on the sentiment seachange which has seen it recover from US$0.7550 in under three weeks.
By 4.55 pm (0555 GMT) the dollar had muscled its way to US$0.7905/10 having leapt to US$0.7880/85 at the opening from US$0.7815/20 late here Monday.

This brought its gains to 1-1/2 cents since Friday's local close of US$0.7750 and included some noteable technical scalps, not least of which was US$0.7850, which added chart kudos to a steadily improving fundamental background.

"The bearish scenario is well and truly out the window," said Clifford Bennett, technical trader at BNP Australia. "The big picture is structurally altered by the break of US$0.7850 -- the immediate risk is a sustainable uptrend developing."
He looked for another few days of upward pressure toward the next major chart target of US$0.7960 followed by a settled consolidation period.
Indeed, he felt the currency could make itself comfortable in a broad US$0.7740/8050 range for some weeks or even months.

The story was the same on the crosses where the dollar drove to five year highs on the Swiss franc and German mark, and even snapped back on the recently buoyant yen to touch a 4-1/2 year peak at 96.34/44, up two big figures on Monday's 94.28/38.
In trade weighted terms it leapt 0.7 point to 60.6, matching its high from December when the dollar was at US$0.8212.

A large part of the strength reflected a transformation in market thinking on domestic interest rates which had seen it swing from discounting an imminent easing to pricing in a 50 basis point hike by the third quarter.
The Reserve Bank began the journey last month by delivering a rousingly upbeat outlook on the economy for 1997, and a string of real data followed to support its view.

Today's figures on retail sales and building approvals were very much in the same vein. Sales leapt 2.7 percent in January to more than make up for a 1.0 percent December drop, while building approvals surged an eyebrow-raising 10.4 percent.
The rise in sales was the largest since March 1994 and well above median forecasts of 1.5 percent.

Approvals for housing construction were biased up by a huge 36.7 percent jump in the apartment sector, which can be very volatile as big developments are approved. These still inject money into the economy, however, as the value of residential building was up almost 11 percent on the month.

"The data are consistent with the view that there will be a significant pickup in growth over the course of this year," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust Australia. "And with the view the RBA has already done enough."
The January data overshadowed Q4 balance of payments figures which showed net exports detracted a chunky one percentage point from expenditure-based GDP in the quarter.
Analysts had pencilled in a deduction of around 0.3 point, so the actual result implied estimates for average GDP would have to be pared back by 0.2 point or so.

The median forecast had been for a rise of 0.6 percent when the data are released on Wednesday. Analysts emphasised this was largely of historical interest given the market was focused on the prospect of future growth.
